issues.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging a completed land acquisition may be refused for unreasonable and unexplained delay where the land has been used for its public purpose and rights of third parties have been created.
material_facts: The landowner filed the writ petition about nine years after publication of the acquisition declaration and about six years after the award, without a sufficient explanation for the delay.
An earlier civil suit sought fresh acquisition proceedings and payment of compensation after subdivision of the land; it did not seek to quash the acquisition notifications.
By the time the writ petition was filed, the acquired land had been developed for a residential scheme, plots and flats had been allotted, and third-party rights had been created.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have refused relief because of laches, even though the acquiring authority had not raised that objection in its affidavits.
issues.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 is discretionary, and unreasonable delay may justify refusal even where no limitation period applies to the writ petition. The limitation period for a comparable civil action is ordinarily a guide to whether delay is unreasonable. Delay in challenging a land acquisition is viewed seriously, especially where the land has been used for the public purpose or third-party rights have accrued. The Court relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai, Ajodhya Bhagat v. State of Bihar, State of Rajasthan v. D.R. Laxmi, Girdharan Prasad Missir v. State of Bihar, Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd., Urban Improvement Trust, Udaipur v. Bheru Lal, Ganpatibai v. State of M.P. and Sawaran Lata v. State of Haryana; it distinguished Vyalikaval Housebuilding Cooperative Society v. V. Chandrappa, involving fraud and mala fides, and Babu Ram v. State of Haryana, where the circumstances did not show negligence or delay.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition and unreasonable_unexplained_delay and (acquired_land_used_for_public_purpose or third_party_rights_created)

predicates.writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition: A person asks a court exercising writ jurisdiction to set aside a land acquisition.
predicates.unreasonable_unexplained_delay: The person waits an unreasonable time to bring the challenge and does not plausibly explain the delay.
predicates.acquired_land_used_for_public_purpose: The acquired land has been put to use for the public purpose for which it was acquired.
predicates.third_party_rights_created: Rights in the developed or allotted land have accrued to people other than the challenger.

issues.definition: When a person brings a land-acquisition writ challenge after unreasonable, unexplained delay and the land has been used for its public purpose or third-party rights have accrued, relief may be denied for laches.

issues.legal_issue: Possession of acquired land may be found to have been taken where the acquiring authorities record its delivery and the subsequent conduct and use of the land support that finding.
material_facts: The authorities recorded that possession of the acquired land had been taken at the site and delivered to the development authority; the record included a field book and a report of a site inspection.
The development authority had deposited 80 percent of the compensation and subsequently constructed roads and utility works, developed the land, and allotted plots and flats.

The landowner disputed that physical possession had been taken, but his earlier pleading referred to the land having been demarcated and to construction being imminent; the Court also considered photographs showing development on the land.
issues.conclusion: The site records and use of the land for the residential scheme established that actual possession had been taken and delivered to the development authority.
issues.legal_principle: There is no hard-and-fast rule for what act constitutes taking possession. For vacant land, going to the site and preparing a panchnama will ordinarily suffice; where crops or structures exist, further steps such as notice and recording possession in the presence of independent witnesses will ordinarily be appropriate. For a large tract, possession may be recorded through an appropriate document rather than by separately taking possession of every parcel. Where a State agency is the beneficiary, 80 percent of the compensation has been deposited and a substantial part of the land has been used for the public purpose, possession may reasonably be presumed. The Court relied on Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M.D. Bhagwat, Balmokand Khatri Educational and Industrial Trust v. State of Punjab, P.K. Kalburqi v. State of Karnataka, NTPC v. Mahesh Dutta, Sita Ram Bhandar Society v. Government of NCT, Delhi, Omprakash Verma v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Brij Pal Bhargava v. State of U.P.

rule.if: public_purpose_acquisition and site_possession_record and (substantial_public_use or advance_compensation_deposited)

predicates.public_purpose_acquisition: The land is acquired for a public purpose, with a public agency or instrumentality as the beneficiary.
predicates.site_possession_record: The authorities go to the land and prepare a record showing that possession was taken or delivered.
predicates.substantial_public_use: A substantial part of the acquired land is used to carry out the public purpose.
predicates.advance_compensation_deposited: The beneficiary deposits a substantial advance portion of the compensation payable for the land.

issues.definition: For a public-purpose acquisition, a site record together with substantial public use or a substantial advance compensation deposit supports treating possession as taken.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition under the urgency procedure does not lapse for failure to make an award within the prescribed period once possession has been taken and the land has vested in the government.
material_facts: The acquisition proceeded under the urgency procedure, and the Court found that possession had been taken and delivered before the award was made.
The award was made more than two years after publication of the acquisition declaration.
The land had been used for the public scheme after possession was taken.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition did not lapse for failure to make the award within two years because possession had been taken under the urgency procedure and the land had vested in the government.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, provides for lapse in the ordinary case when an award is not made within two years of the declaration, before the land has vested in the government. Under Section 17(1), possession may be taken before the award and the land then vests in the government; there is no provision by which land so vested reverts to its owner, so Section 11A does not apply to such an acquisition. The Court relied on Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P. and reiterated the same view in Awadh Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar, Pratap v. State of Rajasthan, Parsinni v. Sukhi, Allahabad Development Authority v. Nasiruzzaman and Government of A.P. v. Kollutla Obi Reddy.

predicates.acquisition_under_urgency_procedure: The land is acquired using a procedure that permits possession to be taken before the award.
predicates.possession_taken_before_award: The authorities take possession of the acquired land before making the award.

issues.definition: When an acquisition uses a procedure permitting early possession and possession is taken before the award, delay in making the award does not cause the acquisition to lapse.
